The dynamics between Jay Gatsby and Daisy Buchanan serve as the central vehicle for F. Scott Fitzgerald’s critique of the American Dream and the illusion of social mobility. Gatsby’s obsession with Daisy is not merely romantic; it is symbolic. He views her as the ultimate prize of his self-made success, a tangible representation of the status and purity he believes he has earned through wealth. However, Daisy is portrayed as shallow, careless, and bound by the rigid class structures of old money. This disconnect highlights the theme of illusion versus reality: Gatsby constructs an idealized version of Daisy and his own past that cannot exist in the real world. Her inability or unwillingness to fully commit to him, and her ultimate retreat into the safety of her marriage with Tom Buchanan, underscores the hollowness of Gatsby’s dream. The corruption of the American Dream is evident in how Gatsby’s pursuit leads him to criminality and moral compromise, suggesting that the dream has been twisted into a mere pursuit of material accumulation rather than genuine happiness or self-improvement. The tragic downfall of Gatsby, therefore, is not just a personal failure but a commentary on the era’s materialistic values, where human connection is commodified and the past is perpetually, futilely sought after.
